title: Setting up a small goat dairy
subtitle: What you need to milk, process, and store goats' milk for your own use.
excerpt: A home goat dairy for personal use needs a clean milking area, basic hygiene equipment, a milk strainer, and refrigeration. Registration as a dairy is only required if you sell milk. For household use and home cheesemaking, a clean routine and rapid chilling are the two things that matter most.
sourceNotes: Jerry Belanger and Sara Thomson Bredesen, Storey's Guide to Raising Dairy Goats (5th edn., 2018). Goat Veterinary Society, Milking Hygiene for Small Flocks (2021). Food Standards Agency, Raw Drinking Milk: What You Need to Know (2022).

glossaryTerms.definition: A raised platform with a head-locking stanchion that holds a goat in position for milking and hoof trimming while freeing both the keeper's hands.
A laboratory test that counts bacteria per millilitre of milk. Not required for home use, but a useful tool if you later sell raw milk.

content.text: A small goat dairy for home use fits in an outbuilding or clean utility room. You need washable surfaces, a milking stand, equipment with no awkward milk traps, and a route to refrigeration within 30 minutes.

A clean, separate area away from the main goat housing is best, but not always possible on a small plot. If milking in the same building, section off a washable corner and clean it before every milking session. Concrete or tiled floors are easier to disinfect than bare earth or wood. A
is strongly recommended: it brings the goat to a comfortable working height, holds the head still in the feed trough, and reduces the effort of each session.
Equipment for a 2 to 4 goat home dairy
Stainless steel milking pail (3 to 5 litre) with a handle and no interior joints where residue can hide.
Milk strainer and disposable filter pads. Single-use pads are more hygienic than reusable cloth for small operations.
Strip cup or dark tray for pre-milking strips.
Teat dip or spray (iodine-based or chlorhexidine-based). Apply post-milking to every teat at every session.
Dairy sanitiser and food-grade detergent. Use an acid wash and an alkaline wash on alternate sessions to prevent mineral build-up and biofilm.
Rinse all equipment with cold water straight after milking, before milk residue sets.
Wash with hot water and food-grade dairy detergent. Scrub all surfaces.
Rinse thoroughly and allow to drain and air-dry inverted. Do not stack wet equipment in a closed cupboard.
Apply a food-grade sanitiser rinse before the next milking session. Do not use this as a substitute for cleaning; it is a final step, not a shortcut.

If you sell raw goats' milk direct to consumers in England, you must register as a milk production holding with the Food Standards Agency and comply with the requirements of Regulation 853/2004 as retained in UK law.
and somatic cell count testing apply. The FSA publishes current guidance on registered raw milk producers on its website.

attrs.cue: Milk has a strong goaty flavour
attrs.cause: Proximity of an intact male (buck) to the milking does, or does under stress during milking
attrs.fix: Keep the buck separated from milking does. The capric and caprylic acids responsible for the goat flavour in milk are significantly elevated when the animals can smell or see a buck. Stress also contributes; maintain a calm milking routine.

attrs.cue: Milk is thickening or curdling in the refrigerator within 24 hours
attrs.cause: High bacterial load from equipment contamination or poor cooling speed
attrs.fix: Check the cleaning and sanitising routine. Ensure milk reaches below 4 C within 30 minutes. Any milk that thickens in this time has a hygiene problem at one of these points.
